blocks.text: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World. Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.
Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.
I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.
By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").

Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.
Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.
This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:

A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]
We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.

My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.

Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:
Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.
These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered:
Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra
[...] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7.
— Ted Sanders, explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions

articles.title: You can just ask AI to do things
articles.titleZh: You can just ask AI to do things
articles.summary: You can just ask AI to do things

blocks.text: One of the most important skills in working with AI is agency: being willing to try new and ambitious things. This is true for what you build, but it’s also true for how you build. AI models are improving so quickly that most of us are bottlenecked1 on noticing that AI agents can help automate particular tasks. Here are some examples of that from my daily work.

Asking the agent to run my dev server. Agents are very good at fixing weird dev environment issues because they work fast, have infinite patience, and have a huge breadth of knowledge. I almost never run the bash commands to start my dev server anymore.

Asking the agent to make requests to my dev server. Part of why I don’t run my dev server manually is that I don’t make requests to it manually either. Instead I’ll say “okay, now start the dev server and run through the happy paths with curl”. The relatively manual process of assembling a set of curl requests and validating the output can now be entirely automated2.

Asking the agent to watch as I make a production change. Every time I do a deploy or flip feature flags, I ask an agent to poll metrics and logs before and after the change. Agents can ingest more logs than I can and are much more patient than me (for instance, I routinely ask for an hourly poll over the rest of the day, which I would not do for most changes on my own).

Asking the agent to get a second opinion from other models. My daily driver is Claude Opus 5.5, which is a good model, but it’s not strictly better than GPT-6-Astra or Gemini Argon3. After I’ve come up with a code change, I typically will say4 “please open subagents to get Astra and Argon’s opinion”. This is made easier by the fact that GitHub Copilot5 has all the top models built in, but I suspect it’d be straightforward enough to ask Claude Code to run a headless Codex session if you’ve got subscriptions to both.

Asking the agent to do a pre-work pass through all my unread messages, logs, and so on. This is one of the most useful things I do, since I work in Australia and my American colleagues start hours before I wake up. I have a scheduled job at 6am every day for an agent to comb through unread messages, identify ones that are asking me questions or have problems I should look at, and do preliminary research (e.g. looking up relevant log lines). That way I can start my workday by scanning that report, which is a big improvement over having to collate everything myself6.

Asking the agent to improve itself. One blocker to a lot of these flows is the pain of setting up the right logs and metrics and Slack MCP servers7, or writing the skills, and so on. But in fact the agent can do all of this itself! Just as it can solve weird problems with your dev server, it can solve weird problems with its own setup. You just have to generate API keys and paste them in the right spots.

Asking the agent to manage its own sessions. If you use a desktop agent tool like GitHub Copilot (or the ChatGPT app, or Claude Code desktop, etc), you will rapidly end up with a spiderweb of sessions and subsessions. It can be tough to identify what are the threads worth picking up. Fortunately, the agent can do this for you as well. I routinely ask it to clear away sessions that haven’t had activity in the last 24 hours, or to catalog my open sessions and suggest ones that can be archived, and so on.

I don’t ask the agent to do everything. I write my own messages and reports (barring some appendices), I make my own design decisions, and I review code myself. This is partly because I think I’m better than models at some of these tasks, and partly because I’m responsible for some of these tasks, so I ought to make the decisions myself. I decide what to work on, and I tend to be ruthless with agent suggestions: of a suggested list of twenty tasks, I’ll often pick zero or one.

However, I do find myself asking the agent to do more and more for me. Often the realization strikes me as obvious: I’ll be doing some mildly tedious task for the hundredth time and think8 “oh wait, I could just get a model to do this for me”, then I’ll never do the task by hand again.

As I’ve said before, I think that model progress could stall out today and we’d still see huge improvements for at least a year as we learn how to use the models we’ve got more effectively.
↩

Why not just have integration tests? Well, often you don’t want to run the same set of operations every time, or you want to jimmy your dev server in order to test some failure mode (e.g. replacing your Redis client with a deliberately broken Redis client).

I haven’t tried Carbon yet.

I will then either scan the top-line feedback from those models myself or let my main agent session incorporate the feedback (depending on how risky the change is).
↩

I work on GitHub Copilot. If you think I have a conflict of interest here, substitute your preferred multi-model agentic coding tool.
↩

I do still read all my unread messages manually. Once I get confident enough in this pre-work report stuff I might stop doing that — it’s a lot of messages.
↩

Some people might not trust the models with Slack or log data, which is fair enough. But if you do, a lot of things get a lot easier.
↩

Or I’ll see someone else getting an agent to do it and realize I could just do the same. I hope one or two of the points in this post can help other people come to that realization.

articles.titleZh: A Health Update From Craig Hockenberry
articles.summary: A Health Update From Craig Hockenberry

blocks.text: I’m writing this post from a hospital bed. And I couldn’t be happier.
You hear folks say chemotherapy sucks, but until you go through it yourself, you don’t really know how bad it can be. It remains a popular activity only because it’s better than the alternative.
My first exposure to chemotherapy was with this contraption: a fluoroscope.

Every week, they used this machine to tap into my spine, extract 5 mg of fluid for analysis, and replace it with 5 mg of methotrexate. There was only a local anesthetic during the procedure and the hardest part was knowing that there was a needle, turned up to eleven, going into my back.

It was afterwards that things got dicey: the nerves in your spine float in a thecal sac filled with spinal fluid that acts as a kind of insulator. Since we were exchanging the fluids, it was easy for the levels to get out of balance and for the nerves to react.
The result were the worst headaches I’ve ever experienced. The good news is that the remedy was simple: to lie flat on my back to ease the pressure gravity was putting on my spine.
That was also the bad news: many days were spent lying prone and trying to avoid boredom. Watching shows and scrolling timelines just doesn’t cut it when that’s all you can do.

Thankfully, the spinal headaches subsided quickly when the six-week course of lumbar punctures finished at the end of January. But my body began to face a new challenge: chemotherapy infusions of Bendamustine and Rituximab.
Everyone experiences chemotherapy differently. Just as every body is different, so is the reaction to the chemicals that are killing the cancer.

The first effect I noticed was in my tastebuds: everything I put in my mouth had a slightly metalic taste, so my eating habits changed. My beloved morning coffee was replaced by tea, food needed a lot less salt, and I started eating a blander diet (cottage cheese with berries remains a favorite).

Some people experience nausea and other gastric issues: luckily, I avoided that. I also didn’t have any hair loss, but my normally thick and curly hair lost its body and became lifeless: an external expression of what was happening to me internally.
As someone who’s always been active and strong, the biggest overall effect of chemo was losing muscle mass and suffering from overall fatigue. It felt very strange to be weak.

I was on a 28 day cycle for my infusions: during the first week I got pumped full of chemicals and then spent three weeks letting my body process them. One of the things they gave me with the infusion on a Tuesday was a dose of steroids that gives the body a boost during the initial onslaught. But by the weekend, that wore off and I felt like shit. It usually took until the middle of the second week before I started feeling human again.

I didn’t lose my appetite, but I wasn’t eating more than normal. The problem was my metabolism was working overtime and my calorie intake didn’t adjust. I lost 50 pounds over the course of a couple of months and eventually got to the point where I was having five meals a day. Too bad it all tasted bad.

One thing that I did to fight my diminished capacity was a daily walk. Anyone who exercises regularly knows that there are always plenty of reasons to avoid it: you didn’t sleep well, you have an important project to finish, or you’re sore from a previous workout. When you’re doing chemo, add feeling like absolute shit to that list.

I still had nerve damage in my spine, so my “walk” was more like a shuffle. Thankfully my wife found some awesome walking sticks to aid with my balance. They are clearly labelled “Not A Medical Device” but they are my most important medical device.

My daily exercise was just like any gym workout: dread at the start, joy at the end. Sometimes there wasn’t much behind that joy: at my lowest point, a walk around the block on flat ground got my heart rate up to 160 bpm. Breathtaking, literally.

That low point was in March. In the week following my infusion, where I was already feeling like crap, I came down with a type of pneumonia that affects people with weakened immune systems. I had no strength and my blood oxygen level plummeted below 90%. Getting from the living room to the kitchen for a drink of water felt like running a marathon, and then my Apple Watch pinged to inform me that I was having an episode of atrial fibrillation. It was a lot and I honestly had thoughts of “is this how it ends?”

Thankfully, antibiotics battled the pneumonia quickly and the chemo effects subsided. My doctor offered to skip the next cycle of chemotherapy, but I decided to push on. There is only one way to be done with a thing.

Throughout all of the infusions, the nerve damage that occurred before the lymphoma discovery didn’t improve. As I said above, my gait and balance were severely compromised: going up and down stairs was particularly challenging. The tingling sensations on my backside and numbness near my abdomen became a bigger concern with each passing month. It wasn’t getting better and I feared it was a permanent condition.

I finished the last of my infusions in May and my body slowly started to recover. Food started tasting better, and my strength and stamina started to return. My daily walks got longer: first a quarter of a mile, then half a mile, then a mile, and then something fantastic happened.

At the end of a walk around our local state park, I went to grab something in the car glovebox. As I did this, I tilted my head forward and the back of my legs lit up with a feeling I had never felt. Something was changing in my spine: and after a couple of weeks it was clear that this was a sign that the nerves were fixing themselves.

Our guess is that the chemotherapy infusions, which attack white blood cells and other parts of the blood that aid in recovery, had retarded the healing in my nervous system. Now that my body had a chance to repair itself, it was.

I can now go up and down stairs without hanging on for dear life. I’m able to walk without aid, but I still like my walking sticks for longer outings since they let me push myself harder. I’ve also started working out in a gym with a trainer: I told him about my stair issues, and now he has me doing them backwards and by hopping on all fours. I am so happy to look like a doofus, and for the continued improvement I’m seeing with exercise.
My regained ability to walk and a stronger immune system allowed me to leave the house. My first night away from home was a short trip to Topanga Canyon to celebrate an August birthday:
After that successful trip, we took a short boat ride to have a nice lunch and look at some kelp. It felt so good to be able to do normal things again.

One lingering part of my life that hasn’t been reestablished is swimming. All the chemotherapy that has been put into my body has been through a port catheter: a small device under my skin that hooks directly into my carotid artery. Getting an infection there would be a very bad thing, and water increases that risk: be it from ocean water full of living organisms or a swimming pool that kids pee in.

With the current El Niño conditions, that’s been a hard thing: the water is warm and “interesting”. My new gym also has a beautiful Olympic-sized pool for lap swimming. I’m happy to be in this hospital bed doing a final stint of chemotherapy because when I’m done, the port is removed.

This last procedure is to make sure there is no lymphoma in my brain fluids: not a difficult or dangerous treatment and the side effects are minimal. But it does require close monitoring because of the high dosages involved.

In six weeks, I’ll be done and spend the winter in that heated pool so that I can finally swim in my beloved Pacific next summer. The buoys are still there, even though the high surf this summer knocked one out!
Last year was hard, and it got worse over time. This year has also been hard, but it’s gotten better with each passing month. For that I’m grateful.

I’m also grateful for my wife Lauren: it’s impossible to imagine making it through all of this without her help, support, and encouragement. The silver lining in all this strife is that it’s made our relationship much stronger. Thanks sweetie!
As with my previous account, there’s an unwanted coda. No matter how hard I try, there’s a complication at the happy ending!

I had typed up everything above as the doctors and nurses prepared me for the first dose of methotrexate. It takes a while for your blood’s pH level to reach a point where the treatment is safe, so I spent much of the day lying in bed, peeing into urine cups, reminiscing about my year, and typing.

Around 10:30 PM, the medication was in my brain and I was trying to wind down for the night (easier said than done when part of the regimen includes steroids). While scrolling through Tapestry, I noticed quite a few posts about a newly announced PHP vulnerability. This caught my attention because we use it for our blogs, an ad server, delivering Kickstarter rewards, and a bunch of other small things.
(This is the point where family that doesn’t understand what I do for a living continues to not understand what I do for a living.)

It quickly became apparent that this was a big deal and something that could allow an attacker access to our server. I had to shut things down before my brain shut down. Thank goodness the steroids held out.
After a couple of hours, I had blocked access to PHP processes in every nook & cranny of our server. After sending a quick message to our Slack explaining how everything was broken, I collapsed.

The next day started with a head and server that were barely working. Our server was out of LTS, so the first order of business was to get it back onto the latest version of Ubuntu using hospital WiFi. It was a good thing my heart rate and blood pressure were being closely monitored.

(Thank goodness for Lish, which proved to be immune to hospital IT shutting down my ssh connection to accept terms & conditions every few hours. There’s also a “I should have my head examined” joke in here somewhere.)
If you noticed that the Iconfactory sites were kinda broken last week, now you know why. It’s because I was kinda broken last week.
Now I’m finishing this post from a comfy chair on our deck. Typing into the latest version of WordPress and PHP. And I couldn’t be happier.

Something was changing in my spine: and after a couple of weeks it was clear that this was a sign that the nerves were fixing themselves.

Our guess is that the chemotherapy infusions, which attack white blood cells and other parts of the blood that aid in recovery, had retarded the healing in my nervous system. Now that my body had a chance to repair itself, it was.

I can now go up and down stairs without hanging on for dear life. I’m able to walk without aid, but I still like my walking sticks for longer outings since they let me push myself harder. I’ve also started working out in a gym with a trainer: I told him about my stair issues, and now he has me doing them backwards and by hopping on all fours. I am so happy to look like a doofus, and for the continued improvement I’m seeing with exercise.
My regained ability to walk and a stronger immune system allowed me to leave the house. My first night away from home was a short trip to Topanga Canyon to celebrate an August birthday:
After that successful trip, we took a short boat ride to have a nice lunch and look at some kelp. It felt so good to be able to do normal things again.

One lingering part of my life that hasn’t been reestablished is swimming. All the chemotherapy that has been put into my body has been through a port catheter: a small device under my skin that hooks directly into my carotid artery. Getting an infection there would be a very bad thing, and water increases that risk: be it from ocean water full of living organisms or a swimming pool that kids pee in.

With the current El Niño conditions, that’s been a hard thing: the water is warm and “interesting”. My new gym also has a beautiful Olympic-sized pool for lap swimming. I’m happy to be in this hospital bed doing a final stint of chemotherapy because when I’m done, the port is removed.

This last procedure is to make sure there is no lymphoma in my brain fluids: not a difficult or dangerous treatment and the side effects are minimal. But it does require close monitoring because of the high dosages involved.

In six weeks, I’ll be done and spend the winter in that heated pool so that I can finally swim in my beloved Pacific next summer. The buoys are still there, even though the high surf this summer knocked one out!
Last year was hard, and it got worse over time. This year has also been hard, but it’s gotten better with each passing month. For that I’m grateful.

I’m also grateful for my wife Lauren: it’s impossible to imagine making it through all of this without her help, support, and encouragement. The silver lining in all this strife is that it’s made our relationship much stronger. Thanks sweetie!
As with my previous account, there’s an unwanted coda. No matter how hard I try, there’s a complication at the happy ending!

I had typed up everything above as the doctors and nurses prepared me for the first dose of methotrexate. It takes a while for your blood’s pH level to reach a point where the treatment is safe, so I spent much of the day lying in bed, peeing into urine cups, reminiscing about my year, and typing.

Around 10:30 PM, the medication was in my brain and I was trying to wind down for the night (easier said than done when part of the regimen includes steroids). While scrolling through Tapestry, I noticed quite a few posts about a newly announced PHP vulnerability. This caught my attention because we use it for our blogs, an ad server, delivering Kickstarter rewards, and a bunch of other small things.
(This is the point where family that doesn’t understand what I do for a living continues to not understand what I do for a living.)

It quickly became apparent that this was a big deal and something that could allow an attacker access to our server. I had to shut things down before my brain shut down. Thank goodness the steroids held out.
After a couple of hours, I had blocked access to PHP processes in every nook & cranny of our server. After sending a quick message to our Slack explaining how everything was broken, I collapsed.

The next day started with a head and server that were barely working. Our server was out of LTS, so the first order of business was to get it back onto the latest version of Ubuntu using hospital WiFi. It was a good thing my heart rate and blood pressure were being closely monitored.

(Thank goodness for Lish, which proved to be immune to hospital IT shutting down my ssh connection to accept terms & conditions every few hours. There’s also a “I should have my head examined” joke in here somewhere.)
If you noticed that the Iconfactory sites were kinda broken last week, now you know why. It’s because I was kinda broken last week.
Now I’m finishing this post from a comfy chair on our deck. Typing into the latest version of WordPress and PHP. And I couldn’t be happier.

blocks.text: An exclusive early look at Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pro—the computer Apple said would never happen.
Photo-Illustration: Jobanny Cabrera; Getty Images

It’s a bright day in Cupertino. Apple’s new CEO strolls to an outdoor seating area within the company’s otherworldly ring-shaped headquarters and pulls up a chair. An employee notes the angle and asks if he minds the sun. John Ternus doesn’t mind at all.

Nearly two months into his tenure, he’s been busy. While the tech world buzzes about AI agents and the upcoming IPO of a company reporting spectacular losses, Ternus’ leadership of a ridiculously profitable firm has so far been defined by a sequence of significant launches—the long-awaited foldable iPhone, a household device that can control digital appliances, new Mac Minis, and AirPods. Intentionally or not, all that activity sends a message that, even as AI dominates the public imagination, hardware products still rule.
Photograph: Shot on iPhone 18 Pro Max by Peter Hapak/Courtesy of Apple

Ternus doesn’t endorse that take, but he doesn’t object when I suggest it. “We’ve been working on these products for quite some time,” he says. “It feels like everyone here is just kind of riding high right now, enjoying it.”
I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.
Ternus beams. “Who knew?”

We are referring to the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that Apple is releasing today at an event in Los Angeles. It’s got a mighty M5 Pro or M5 Max chip and a show-stopping tandem OLED screen. (A tandem screen has multiple light-emitting layers, producing more dramatic contrasts.) But its most conspicuous feature is one that’s been deeply woven into iPhones, iPads, and even Apple Watches for years but not Apple’s laptops: a touch display. After years of resistance, a Mac screen has finally gone digital. As in fingers.

This turnaround is a big deal to Apple fans. Ternus shrugs off the drama. “The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”

Ternus and Apple want to make sure that the Mac faithful don’t panic that the 42-year-old franchise is losing its identity to Apple’s gangbusters mobile products. “We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”
Photograph: Courtesy of Apple

Apple has a long history of refusing to implement certain desirable features, only to pivot when it feels the time is right. Steve Jobs once proclaimed iPods would never do video, until they did. He also once said “no one’s going to buy” a jumbo-size phone—and then Apple released a supersized iPhone 6. Then there was that time Jobs declared styluses inappropriate for tablets. Now the Apple Pencil works with iPads and the brand-new Duo.

The 2026 MacBook Pro instantly qualifies as the canonical example of this switcheroo. Apple executives had been on record regarding touch on PCs as a misbegotten idea. Never mind that just about every PC maker not headquartered in Cupertino has implemented touch on their laptops. And customers of Microsoft, Dell, Acer, Lenovo, and HP have snapped them up. Clearly, people wanted touch on their laptop displays. Even toddlers knew it—put some rug rats in front of a computer and their little arms shoot straight to the screen in futile attempts to swipe and scroll as they do on their iPads. People were baffled why Apple—the pioneer in touch displays since the iPhone—was so steadfast in its rejection.

In 2015, while doing a story about a new iMac, I pressed Phil Schiller, then the senior vice president of worldwide product marketing, on this very question. Usually, top Apple executives field such queries with cryptic remarks. In this case, Schiller began a filibuster. “I’m going to get a little bit philosophical,” he said, then launched into what I later described as the Grand Unified Theory of Apple Hardware.

He explained that every Apple hardware product—the Watch, iPad, iMac, MacBook—is basically a computer and a piece of glass. Each one has a specific function. And each one has an interface appropriate to the hardware. Multitouch is fine for products like the iPhone, he said—but not the Macintosh. He provided two reasons: ergonomics and the software interface.

“From the ergonomic standpoint, we have studied this pretty extensively, and we believe that on a desktop scenario, where you have a fixed keyboard, having to reach up to do touch interfaces is uncomfortable,” he told me.

As for the interface, Schiller argued that Apple’s two main operating systems were built on different design principles. The iPhone and iPad’s iOS was multitouch from the get-go, and didn’t use macOS conventions that require precision, such as cursors and tiny boxes to close windows. “These two worlds are different on purpose, and that’s a good thing—we can optimize around the best experience for each of those and not try to mesh them together into a least-common-denominator experience,” he told me.

A year later, when Apple introduced a MacBook Pro with the ill-fated “touch bar”—a dynamic strip of virtual function keys above the keyboard’s top row—Schiller doubled down on the view that touch should never find its way into a Mac display. He said that such a move would mean totally redesigning the menu bar for fingers, and that would clash with the experience of pointer devices like a touchpad or mouse. “You can’t optimize for both,” he said.

To double-check this assumption, Apple conducted user tests with touchscreens on Mac. “What the heck, we could be wrong,” Schiller told me then. “We’ve absolutely come away with the belief that it isn’t the right thing to do. Our instincts were correct.”

When I met with Apple executives Johny Srouji and Greg Joswiak this week to discuss the touchscreen MacBook Pro, you bet I invoked Schiller’s list of concerns. (Apple’s reps chose not to make Schiller, who now holds the title of “Apple Fellow,” available for an interview. In fact, they laughed when I asked.) It wasn’t only Schiller drawing a red line. In 2021, Ternus told journalist Joanna Stern, “The Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven’t really felt a reason to change that.”

“Ten years is a very, very long time,” says Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer. “Many things have changed, whether it's the display technology, the custom silicon, et cetera.” Eventually, he told me, the confluence of chips, display tech, and software architecture “met our bar.” “I like my engineers to be gated by physics, not imagination or timelines,” he says.

Joswiak, who holds Schiller’s old title of SVP of worldwide marketing, concedes that touch was overdue, at least for users with sophisticated needs. Its pro customers—engineers, scientists, software developers, and media creators—were impatient with Apple for its failure to let them interact directly with the screen. “Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone,” Joswiak says. “So this is something that they’re natural with. There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.”

Between the lines, Srouji and Joswiak seem to consider their competitors’ touchscreen implementations shabby and lazy. The Apple ethos, as every one of its executives will happily explain to anyone who asks, is an expectation of quality that’s sky-high. “If you’re working on something easy, you’re wasting your time,” says Srouji, who has been at Apple since 2008 and has pretty much driven its innovation by spearheading the company’s charge to custom-build silicon.

“The easy things, I want to outsource,” he continues. “So the custom silicon is hard. The touch is hard. The display is hard. Everything we build is hard.” This swaggering philosophy dates from the Steve Jobs days and, in 2026, stands in contrast to the endgame of the ascendant AI industry, which hopes to turn over the toughest parts of industrial production to superintelligent entities.

Srouji presents Mac touch as a suite of innovations, starting with that screen that Ternus described as the Mac’s best ever. It also involves custom silicon and a rearchitected thermal system to prevent the display from feeling hot when people pinch, stretch, and swipe on it. Srouji contends that current touchscreen laptops suffer from “wobble” when fingers make contact with the display; to minimize this effect, Apple has redesigned the hinge on the MacBook Pro screen to stabilize it.

When I get a demo of the 16-inch version (as with previous Pros, it’s also available in a 14-inch version), I see what they mean about the display. It’s noticeably dense and bright, and the obsidian blacks are the deepest I’ve seen on a computer screen. In part because the OLED screen doesn’t require backlighting, this MacBook weighs less than its predecessor.
Photograph: Courtesy of Apple

As a pair of Apple managers take the MacBook through its paces, I see how Apple has addressed some of Schiller’s decade-old concerns, like having to redesign the menu bar for fingers. While it looks the same, when you move a finger over a menu item, it expands to allow you to select your choice with precision. Some of the objects on the screen, like the traffic-light buttons that close or hide windows, also get bigger when you touch them.

They show me how the touch tech can handle precision tasks, like color grading in the video editing software DaVinci Resolve, or tweaking a soundtrack on Logic Pro, Apple’s high-end audio workstation. One innovation, not just for pros, is a new gesture to pull down the “Dynamic Island,” that black oval hosting ongoing tasks that has made its way to Mac from iPhone. An expanded version floats on the screen like a widget, enabling easy access to Siri responses and Spotlight search.
But what about greasy fingers messing up the screen? I was told that the new display has an anti-reflective outer coating that will require no more cleaning than your normal non-interactive screen.

Apple clearly hopes that the MacBook Pro launch puts an exclamation point on the burst of product announcements that Apple customers are still absorbing. For the foldable Duo, some customers are impatiently waiting for delivery dates that stretch into January. (Lines were long at Apple stores last Friday, when the device went on sale, and Joswiak personally greeted those who queued up at Apple’s Fifth Avenue store in New York City.)

I ask Srouji whether Apple is making a statement with its armada of new products, maybe as a way to say that in a year dominated by AI obsession, Apple is still here. He responds much as his new boss did, contending that Apple is simply sticking to its game plan. “We’re here to build the most amazing products in the world, and we want to ship them when we believe it’s ready and complete,” says Srouji. “That’s the statement we’re making. I think everyone knows we’re here.”

While longtime users will be happy to hear that a Macintosh now has a touchscreen, those with limited budgets will be disappointed. Apple’s current stance—that touch-on-a-Mac display is most appropriate to the “pro” crowd—rationalizes an astronomical price tag: The new MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. Financial analyst Neil Cybart, who got an early MacBook Pro briefing, thinks that serious professionals will pay up. “People are in search of value, and that means going for products that leverage technology to improve what they’re doing,” he says.

When I ask Ternus about the timeline, or even the possibility, of seeing touch displays on less exorbitantly priced MacBook Airs and iMacs, he shakes his head. “You’ve been doing this a long time,” he says. “You know I will never tell you anything about our future.”

I don’t know why I bothered to ask. If Ternus said that touch would never happen on a MacBook Air, who would believe him? I’d be back at The Ring a year later, hearing that Apple had finally figured out a way to do it right.

With my kids I’m currently building a little dungeron
crawler and we’re trying to
learn a bit about game
development along the way.
However given that we live in the modern times of increasing capabilities we
wanted to get a narrator and voice over.

But we also wanted it to not sound like everyone’s standard AI voices so I
looked into what options there are on the table.  After some investigation I
narrowed down to using Qwen3-TTS which
uses voice embeddings for custom voices.

With a bit of creativity you can also do more with those custom voices than
appears initially.  In case this is of interest to you, this post just covers
what we learned and with some examples.  You can probably point your agent to
it and it can do something with it.
What Qwen Offers

Qwen3 is not the only TTS model in town, and it wans’t even my first choice.  We
initially used Kokoro.  However
Qwen3 supports voice cloning and we wanted to have it feel a bit more unique.
In practice it’s a bit tricker though. Qwen3 ships three kinds of models:
1.7B-Base (and 0.6B): clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio
1.7B-CustomVoice: comes with nine built-in speakers and instructions
1.7B-VoiceDesign: invents a voice from a text description

The base model clones either in context or from the speaker embedding alone but
there is no documented way to clone a voice and direct it with instructions.
That means unlike the custom voice and voice design models you cannot say “speak
sad” or “whisper” with a cloned base model.

At present the official options for a custom voice are fine-tuning Base on a
single speaker or to make a clip with VoiceDesign and clone it with Base.  That
is not all that bad, but it means instructions are gone.
Playing With It

For this blog post I took 28 seconds of me from my talk at PyAI
Conf, cut between two pauses so
that it starts and ends on a full sentence, and transcribed it with Whisper.
The transcript is really only needed for baking but to compare against an
already existing voice it’s useful to have it say the same thing as the original
recording.

blocks.text:
A small-scale rule of thumb. This article will land much better with a concrete
example, but I am drawing a blank here, so you gotta just blindly trust my say
so!

When implementing a software module, it’s often a case that you are writing a
public function foo, and at least part of what foo does is already handled
by another public function bar. The DRY instinct encourages you to call
bar() from within foo. This usually creates problems down the line. Instead,
create a new private function and refactor both foo and bar to call that
shared helper:

Rationale: the goal of a public API is to provide an interface that works best
at the call site. If parts of public API are re-used to implement the rest of
the API, then there’s a tension between making the interface convenient for the
outside user and making it convenient to use from within abstraction itself.
Namely, functions tend to grow optional parameters that should never be set by
the user. Crucially, the parameter growth and interface degradation can happen
after the original code sharing.

By proactively making the shared implementation private, the tension is defused.
You still might need to tinker with helper signature until it does everything
it needs to do, but, because the helper is private, this is a cheap, local
change.

A notable exception to this rule of thumb are “shortcut” APIs, where a public
function is defined as a commonly used chain of calls to other public
functions. There, the rule is the opposite — no private calls are allowed,
to make sure that it is a genuine shortcut, and not a midlayer mistake.

P.S. While researching if anyone wrote a better blog post already, I stumbled
upon a fun stack overflow question, asking, paraphrasing:

I’ve heard that it is bad when a public function calls another public
function. Is this really so?

The most upvoted answer explains that it is indeed bad, because this makes
mocking to test a single method in isolation more complicated. Which is, imo, a
natural, but horrible consequence of misguided approach to testing. You
shouldn’t be mocking your methods, you should mock your IO. And, similarly, you
shouldn’t test methods, but rather software functionality (unless you are
building a public library with a stable API, which is a fun and important, but
very narrow fraction of software development).

The accepted answer says that this recommendation makes no sense if it is not
backed by an industry wide or an organizational standard. Which somehow manages
to make even less sense — you shouldn’t follow the guideline rules because
they are written in sanctified ink! Rather, you should apply each particular
rule because of the underlying reasons that motivate the rule. Guidelines and
best practices articles can concentrate lots of good reasoning in a single
place, but they don’t absolve you from thinking!

Much of modern civilization is built on top of chemical reactions, either to produce new materials (as in the blast furnace, which converts iron oxide into metallic iron), or to generate energy. Chemical reactions, as we’ve previously noted, work by rearranging how atoms hold their outermost electrons. Combine an atom of sodium and an atom of chlorine, for instance, and sodium’s outermost electron will end up in chlorine’s outer electron shell in an ionic bond, creating sodium chloride — common table salt.

With these sorts of chemical reactions, we’re only shifting around atoms and the electrons that orbit them in the form of chemical bonds. The interior of the atom — the atomic nucleus, which contains an atom’s protons and neutrons — remains unchanged. But if you create the right conditions, it’s possible to rearrange the interior of atoms as well. In nuclear fission, the reaction that powers nuclear power plants, the nucleus of an atom splits, creating several new atoms and releasing an enormous amount of energy in the process. In the fusion reaction taking place within the sun, hydrogen atoms are fused together, their individual nuclei combining to form helium. In particle accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider, charged particles are accelerated into each other using electromagnetic fields, and scientists study the various fragments created by the collisions.

By changing the number of protons or neutrons in the nucleus, these nuclear reactions can create things that can’t be created via conventional chemistry. Change the number of neutrons in an atom, and you get a new isotope of that particular element: an atomic variant of the same chemical, but with a different mass. Change the number of protons, and you end up with a different element entirely, possibly one that doesn’t occur in nature at all.

Typically, the products of these reactions (which we’ll simply refer to as “isotopes”) are unstable: they decay into some other, more stable isotope, emitting radiation in the process, which can be harnessed for various purposes. Carbon dating, for example, relies on the fact that living organisms absorb carbon-14, an isotope of carbon with eight neutrons in the nucleus that eventually and reliably decays into atomically stable nitrogen-14 (the “14” indicates the number of protons and neutrons — carbon-14 has six protons and eight neutrons, while nitrogen-14 has seven protons and seven neutrons). Another process, radiographic welding inspection, uses a variety of radioactive isotopes, such as iridium-192 and selenium-75, to emit gamma rays to inspect welds. Smoke detectors rely on americium-241, an isotope of the artificial element americium — radiation emitted by a small amount of americium causes an electric current to flow across a chamber, but if smoke enters the chamber, the flow of electricity is interrupted, triggering an alarm.

Currently, our use of isotopes is constrained by the fact that creating them is difficult and expensive. Gram for gram, isotopes are some of the most expensive materials on the planet. And the supply chains to produce them are often extremely fragile. Technetium-99m1, a widely used radioactive isotope for medical imaging, is produced through the decay of  another radioactive isotope, molybdenum-99. Molybdenum-99, in turn, is produced in only a few nuclear reactors around the world;there was a worldwide shortage in 2024 when some of these reactors went offline for repairs. If isotopes could be manufactured more easily and more cheaply, it could open up numerous possibilities — cheaper medical treatments, better nuclear power sources, possibly even useful new materials.
We’re all familiar with the periodic table, which lists every chemical element known to man.

Each element on the periodic table has an atomic number, which is the number of protons in the nucleus, starting from atomic number 1 (hydrogen, which has one proton in the nucleus) all the way up to atomic number 118 (oganesson, an artificial element with 118 protons in the nucleus). It’s the number of protons in an atom that makes an element an element — carbon always has six protons, because having six protons in the nucleus of an atom is what makes that atom carbon.

But there are also neutrons in the nucleus, and the number of neutrons can vary. Most carbon on Earth, for instance, is carbon-12, which has six protons and six neutrons. But about 1% of carbon is carbon-13, which has seven neutrons. The most common isotope of helium is helium-4, which has two neutrons, but there’s also helium-3, which only has one. Most of the water molecules in Earth’s oceans are made up of hydrogen with no neutrons (hydrogen-1), but about one out of every 3200 water molecules contains a hydrogen with one neutron, also known as deuterium (water made from deuterium is sometimes known as “heavy water”).
We can visualize isotopes on what’s called a nuclide chart, shown below. The horizontal axis is the number of neutrons in a nucleus, while the vertical axis is the number of protons.

We can see that most elements have several different isotopes, most of which are unstable. Only the isotopes in black in the chart above are stable; everything else will eventually decay. Red isotopes on the chart above decay by what’s known as “beta-plus” decay or electron capture, turning a proton into a neutron. Teal isotopes decay by “beta-minus” decay, turning a neutron into a proton. Yellow isotopes decay by “alpha” decay, emitting an alpha particle (two protons and two neutrons). The rate at which an isotope decays into another isotope is typically described as its “half-life” — the amount of time it takes for half of a sample to undergo radioactive decay. Half-lives can vary wildly, from tiny fractions of a second for hydrogen-5 to hundreds of millions of years for uranium-235.

For isotopes that are stable, or that decay slowly enough that they can be found in the environment, it’s sometimes possible to obtain them by separating them out from other isotopes. But this is often difficult, because isotopes tend to be chemically identical, and most separation methods must rely on minute differences in the atoms’ weights. Much of the difficulty in the Manhattan Project, for instance, was in creating sufficient concentrations of a specific isotope of uranium, uranium-235, that would undergo nuclear fission. Uranium-235 only makes up about 0.72% of natural uranium, and producing a single, football-sized lump of it required a processing facility the size of a small city.

But many isotopes can’t be found in nature at all. There’s no natural source of the technetium-99m or molybdenum-99 used for medical imaging, or the selenium-75 used for welding inspection. It’s thus useful to be able to manufacture specific isotopes.
How do we do this?

At a high level, creating isotopes means rearranging the interior of an atom. In some cases, this happens by natural radioactive decay. The americium-241 used in smoke detectors, for instance, mostly comes from decaying plutonium-241. But for most isotopes we’re interested in, we can’t rely on natural mechanisms; instead, we have to deliberately rearrange atomic nuclei by bombarding them with different sorts of particles. Depending on the sort of particle you hit the nucleus with, the energy of that particle, and the nature of the target atom, you can create different sorts of reactions. These reactions are typically described by the following format: target(input particle, released particle)product. So in 1917 when Rutherford bombarded nitrogen atoms with alpha particles, producing oxygen and hydrogen nuclei (protons), that reaction was N-14(alpha,p)O-17. The figure below shows different sorts of reactions and how they move an atom to a different location on the nuclide chart.

There are a few different ways we can hit an atom with a particle. One is to use a particle accelerator, such as the cyclotron, invented in 1929 by Ernest Lawrence (who would go on to win a Nobel Prize for his invention). The cyclotron uses powerful electromagnetic fields to accelerate charged particles along spiral paths. With his 27-inch particle accelerator, Lawrence could accelerate helium nuclei to roughly 1% of the speed of light.

It wasn’t long after Lawrence created his cyclotron that it began to be used to create various isotopes. Naturally occurring radium was already being used to treat cancer with radiation, and Lawrence hired personnel to investigate the potential of using cyclotron-created isotopes for medical and research purposes, such as radioactive phosphorus-32. Phosphorus-32, which has one more neutron than the stable phosphorus-31, was a promising research isotope because organisms naturally incorporate and accumulate phosphorus: if that phosphorus were radioactive, it would allow various metabolic pathways to be observed and possibly allow for highly targeted radiation treatments. Lawrence quickly found that demand for phosphorus-32 for experimental cancer treatments and biological research was “almost insatiable,” and by 1939 a dozen cancer patients had been treated with cyclotron-produced phosphorus-32.

Particle accelerators are still used to produce isotopes today. GE Healthcare, for instance, sells several different medical cyclotrons. The GE PETtrace 800 uses a beam of hydrogen or deuterium nuclei (protons or proton + neutron) to create isotopes such as oxygen-15, nitrogen-13, and fluorine-18, which are then used for medical imaging.

I don’t know why I started to put this together. These machines fascinate me,
because so much of early computing/hacker type culture happened on them. I
started writing a table, but realised a timeline would be more intuitive. In
this graph, the price is for a minimal configuration and adjusted for inflation.
The time is the memory cycle time, a decent proxy for speed.
Some notes:

The pdp-1 was created mostly as an experiment. At the time, industrial
control systems used either humans or complicated contraptions of logic boards
to make decisions. Some engineers at dec wanted to see if there was a
customer base willing to use general-purpose computers instead.11 But
it wasn’t called a computer then, because the word “computer” back then meant
big mainframe systems that ran batch calculations.

The pdp-4 was a variant of pdp-1 that was a little slower and much
cheaper. It was not compatible with the pdp-1. The pdp-4 was upgraded with
new chip technology and became the pdp-7, which was then optimised further
for cost and speed and became the pdp-9.

The pdp-5 was created when they realised the pdp-1 and pdp-4 machines
were overkill for industrial control systems. By being smaller, it could be
much cheaper, at the cost of compatibility with pdp-1 and pdp-4. It was
still intended for roughly the same market. The chip upgrade turned it into
the pdp-8.

The pdp-6 was a completely different beast, aimed at a different market. It
supported having tonnes of directly-addressable memory, as well as memory
protection, so it could be used as a time-sharing system. The amount of memory
made it run Lisp well.22 The smaller machines could also run Lisp, but not
large Lisp programs. With the chip upgrade, it became the pdp-10.

The pdp-11 was a new architecture again, intended to subsume all the
previous models, to avoid running three incompatible lines in parallel. There
were many variants of the pdp-11, with various performance characteristics
and corresponding price points. However, even its most powerful configuration
wasn’t powerful enough to attract many pdp-10 users.

The vax came much later, but it’s included in the table anyway because it is
what eventually subsumed the pdp-10. The vax was somewhat compatible with
the pdp-11, but they served different markets.

There is a noticeable split in the hacker culture between users of the smaller
(18 bit and less) and larger (32 bits and more) computers, exemplified by the
contrast between Unix and Emacs. Unix was first created on pdp-7, then ported
to pdp-11, then distributed to other pdp-11 users. The fact that it needed
to run on these smaller machines, and still handle time sharing, shaped much of
its implementation and interface. The same thing is true of the C language and
standard library. Then we have something like Emacs, which was created on the
massive pdp-10, and gained popularity with other pdp-10 users. It had plenty
of hardware resources to use, and it did. The same thing is true of many Lisp
variants.

What decided whether you became a small-computer hacker or large-computer hacker

I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses, the master builder of New York. His books are widely regarded as the best explorations of political power that have ever been written.

They also happen to be literally my favorite books ever.  Whenever I meet somebody new, one of the first questions they ask me is, “Who is it that you most want to interview that you haven’t yet?” And for six years, I’ve answered the question the same way: Robert Caro.
I’ve spent so much time trying to make this interview happen: chasing his agent, calling his publisher, contacting the museums that have his archives, and even sending him handwritten letters.
I finally got to sit down with him, and I’m very happy with how it turned out. It’ll be out this Friday.
In the meantime, as I was preparing for the interview, and rereading these biographies, I wrote down the lessons they laid out about how to accumulate and use power.

Robert Moses was the master builder of New York. He built more of the physical city than anyone before or since: the Triborough and Verrazano bridges, the Cross Bronx Expressway, Jones Beach, Lincoln Center, Shea Stadium, two giant power dams upstate, in addition to hundreds of parks and dozens of pools. Of the 899 miles of highways completed in New York State by 1964, Moses had built 672 of them. His projects collectively cost hundreds of billions of dollars in today’s money.

For more than 30 years, Robert Moses was the most powerful person in New York (more powerful than any elected mayor or governor, despite not being elected to anything). How did he get and keep that much power?

Part of the answer is that Moses wrote the laws that governed him. He was called ‘the best bill drafter in Albany,’ and he used that skill to write himself powers that the legislators voting on his bills didn’t know they were granting.

The political genius of Robert Moses is perhaps best illustrated by his use of public authorities, which are government-created corporations that build city infrastructure. Public authorities sell bonds to pay for a specific project, say a new bridge. Once the bridge is built, the authority would charge drivers a toll until it had collected enough money to pay off its bonds. Then the authority would tear down the tollbooths, hand the bridge over to the city, and go out of existence.

At least, that was the idea. And that’s what Albany assumed would happen when the New York State Legislature approved the Triborough Bridge Authority Act of 1933, whose final version included - buried within pages and pages of legalese - a few seemingly minor alterations drafted by Robert Moses.

Section 1 clearly stated that the authority would dissolve once the bonds were paid off.  And since the bonds could run at most 40 years (and the revenues from the bridge would pay back the initial cost far sooner), it seemed like the authority had a clear, built-in expiration date. However, in a subsection of Section 9, Moses added a single sentence that said the Authority could “from time to time” pay off its old bonds by issuing new ones. And those new ones could be “for any other corporate purpose.” So just before the original bonds were about to expire, the authority now had the right to issue a totally fresh 40 year note, for a potentially totally different use.

And what could the Authority build with all that money? The original act let it build two bridges and their “approaches.” Moses’ amendments also gave this authority the right to build “connecting” roads and “facilities not inconsistent with the use of the project”. These rights, when interpreted as creatively as Moses intended to, would allow Moses to alter most of the roads, parks, and housing in New York - for if a road connected to a road which connected to a road which connected to the bridge, or if a park lay along the road that connected to the road that connected to the road that connected to the bridge, surely the Triborough Authority was entitled to improve and change it.

All this construction could be financed by the bridges’ enormous toll revenues and the right of the Triborough Authority to borrow against them. To give some perspective, in 1946, the entire New York City government could only borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit. That very same year, Triborough could borrow $360 million. So Moses’ bridge authority had access to more than double the amount of money as the largest city in America.

But what if a future governor or mayor eventually learned about all the power and revenue that had been delegated to this authority, and decided to claw back? Moses had planned for that too, and his solution was so clever that no lawyer or lawmaker in Albany saw it coming. The US Constitution says that no state shall make “any … Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts” entered into by a government entity. A bond issued by a public authority is such a contract. Moses snuck a clause into the law that allowed him to add into those bond contracts “any other matters, of like or different character, which in any way affect the security or protection of the bonds”. These “matters” included whether Triborough could charge tolls for however long they wanted, and whether they would get to keep the surplus thus generated.

That is to say, Moses could now entrench his powers simply by writing them into the bonds he issued. From the moment the bonds were sold, those powers could no longer be revoked by the Legislature, the governor, or the mayor - by anything, in fact, short of a Constitutional Convention. The powers that Moses now had were guaranteed for the bonds’ entire lifetime - a lifetime which could always be extended simply by refinancing.

So, with just a few minor tweaks, Moses turned an act meant to allow the construction of two bridges into the basis of an institution that could build basically anything it wanted anywhere in New York (and whose authority to do so was protected by the U.S. Constitution).

These bond covenants had turned Triborough Authorities’ power into granite, but nothing in them guaranteed that Robert Moses would remain as chairman. So how did Moses retain his position for 30 years?

Part of the answer is, again, the law. Moses drafted the Triborough act so that its commissioners could be removed mid-term only “on stated charges after a formal hearing.” But any differences he had with a mayor or governor were more about what he decided to build and whom he displaced to build it, rather than personal conduct.

As Caro says, “Robert Moses was not himself corrupt. He was, in fact, as uninterested in obtaining payoffs for himself as any public servant who ever lived. In the politicians’ phrase, he was ‘money honest.’”

So, there were never any formal charges to bring. But this only explains why he wasn’t fired in the middle of his term. Why was he reappointed every six years? Well, at his peak, Moses was a hydra with a dozen heads. He held 12 different government posts at the same time: city construction coordinator, chairman of the State Council of Parks, chairman of the State Power Authority, and so on. Some of these positions were appointed by the mayor, some by the governor, so no single person could cut off all his heads simultaneously. And removing him from any one position meant making an enemy of the man who would still be the most powerful person in New York.

More importantly, no mayor or governor wanted to fire him. The way we remember Robert Moses today is based on a reputation that calcified in the 1970s, when The Power Broker came out and New York was experiencing a dark age of crime, deindustrialization, and white flight. Moses got much of the blame (the subtitle of The Power Broker is “Robert Moses and the Fall of New York”). In my opinion, that crisis had more to do with large structural factors than with Moses himself - cities he had nothing to do with, like Detroit and St. Louis, experienced a much more dramatic collapse.

For the vast majority of his career, Moses was incredibly popular. In the 1930s and 1940s, New York high schools voted Moses ‘the most admired New Yorker’. This was because he had delivered, over and over again, public works which millions of New Yorkers got to use and enjoy: beaches, parks, pools, and playgrounds, as well as the bridges and the parkways that let families drive out to them. And he did so at a speed and a scale that nobody had seen before: in just his first four months as the city’s Park Commissioner, by keeping crews working around the clock, he finished 1,700 park renovations. And he did it all without a whiff of personal scandal.

As Caro writes in The Power Broker, “[I]t was not unusual at park and playground opening ceremonies for children, prodded by their parents, to break into the cheer ‘Two, four, six, eight—who do we appreciate? Mr. Moses! MR. MOSES!! MR. MOSES!!!’”

Importantly, Moses could deliver these enormous and popular public works within a timeframe that fit into a single election cycle. If a mayor gave Robert Moses the power to build something, he could expect to be standing at the ribbon-cutting for it before he was up for re-election. Today, it’s almost unimaginable that the government could construct something big in a year or two. For example, construction on the Second Avenue subway in New York began in 1972; the first section was opened in 2017, and just these initial 2 miles cost  taxpayers $4.5 billion.

A lot of the funding for public works comes from Washington - cities that receive the most money are the ones who have already finalized their blueprints and can break ground as soon as a new federal initiative is announced. Moses had the largest and best team of planners and engineers in the country. And because of that, by 1936, New York was getting one-seventh of the money that the federal government had set aside for Depression era work-relief… for the entire nation. And the projects this funding was going towards were the ones chosen by Moses. If the mayor had some different idea about what should be constructed, he’d have to draw up his own plans, which he didn’t have the independent technical expertise to do. So he could either build the projects that Moses wanted to build or build nothing at all.

Between his popularity, his unique ability to get things done, and his control over money, Moses had a lot of leverage. And he was not shy about using it. Far from being worried about getting fired, Moses would constantly threaten to quit whenever he didn’t get his way. Under Mayor Wagner, one aide said, “it seemed like he was resigning about one thing or another about twice a day.” He threatened resignation to La Guardia so often, over such small things, that La Guardia’s lawyer got a stack of forms printed that read “I, Robert Moses, do hereby resign as…”, to save Moses the trouble of writing it out every time.

Behind that joke was real fear. If a mayor accepted that resignation, not only would he be forfeiting completion of whatever projects Moses was working on (along with the money apportioned for those projects), he’d also be picking a public fight with the most respected official in all of New York. Moses had spent years befriending the owners of the city’s newspapers - he spent weekends at the summer home of the Sulzbergers, the family that owned the New York Times. The mayor knew that if Moses resigned, the next morning, all the front pages would tell the story of how the man above politics was driven out by a craven politician because he refused to compromise the city’s interests.
And the power that Moses derived from his popularity with the masses was nothing compared to the power he derived from his connections with New York’s powerful private interests.

We are very used today to NIMBY, where powerful but concentrated interest groups manage to stymie projects despite their broad popularity. Moses built a concentrated faction for YIMBY. He built a graft machine that greased the wheels for new construction, because it ensured the most influential people in the state would all benefit whenever a project got underway.

The banks got to buy his bonds at a steep discount without competitive bidding, the unions got more jobs, politically connected lawyers got legal fees, and party bosses got paid to broker insurance policies on bridges that had no plausible risk of falling down. Moses could then rely on these beneficiaries to call up anyone who stood in the way of one of his projects, whether that was a borough president or the governor himself.

Caro paints Moses as someone who began as an idealist, rather than someone who craved power from the start. In the 1910s, Moses was a brilliant young reformer who joined this new “good government” movement, which was trying to replace Tammany Hall’s patronage with honest and competent administration. He spent years fighting the machine. But his reforms got killed - the machine won. Moses learned that ideals are useless without the power to realize them. Caro writes:

In the beginning—and for decades of his career—the power Robert Moses amassed was the servant of his dreams, amassed for their sake, so that his gigantic city-shaping visions could become reality. But power is not an instrument that its possessor can use with impunity. It is a drug that creates in the user a need for larger and larger dosages. And Moses was a user.

Lyndon Johnson’s story, on the other hand, is kind of the opposite. For most of his career, there was little evidence he had a coherent political ideology - he was a ruthless power-seeker who embraced whatever happened to be most expedient at the time. When Johnson first entered the U.S. Senate, he realized that the most powerful men there were conservative Southern Dixiecrats. And the Johnson that they encountered was one who had molded himself to their form.

While writing Master of the Senate, Caro interviewed former Georgia Senator Herman Talmadge. He asked Talmadge what impression he got from freshman Senator Lyndon Johnson about the proper relationship between white people and black people.

“Master and servant.” So I [Caro] asked, Well didn’t Johnson have any sympathy for blacks, any desire to improve their lot? My notes say “long pause.” And then I wrote [Talmadge’s] two-word reply: “None indicated.” Another pause, and then: “He was with us in his heart. I believed him. I believed him.”
Of course, we know that once he became president, Johnson spearheaded the 1964 Civil Rights Act and the 1965 Voting Rights Act, the most important civil rights laws since Reconstruction.

So Moses began as a naive idealist but, in Caro’s telling, became someone seeking power for its own sake. Johnson was an ambitious opportunist from the very start, and it was only once he had real power that he used it for ideals few knew he had.
Lyndon Johnson was the most powerful Senate majority leader - perhaps the most powerful legislator period - in the history of this country. Here’s Caro in Master of the Senate:
He was master of the Senate—master of an institution that had never before had a master, and that at the time, almost half a century later, when this book is being written, has not had one since.

No leader before Johnson had wielded this kind of power, because the Senate had been deliberately set up by the founders to not be “led”. When Johnson asked the Library of Congress for a list of the Majority Leader’s formal powers, he found that there was only one: the right to be recognized first on the floor. Before Johnson, the Majority Leader was less a leader and more a lightning rod. He’d be blamed in the national press and in his home state for everything the Senate failed to do, yet he had no actual power to do anything about those failures. Being in this predicament was so politically toxic that Johnson’s two predecessors as majority leaders had both lost their own Senate seats.

A big part of the reason that Johnson became his party’s leader at just 44, in a Senate whose average age was around 60, was that hardly anyone else wanted such a thankless and useless job. And in their hands, this job would have remained useless. But they were not Lyndon Johnson.
Johnson turned himself into the second most powerful man in America (right behind the president) in three different ways.

Johnson transformed the Senate’s rules, institutions and norms so that he alone had the power to grant important favors to his colleagues. If a senator needed a bill passed, Johnson was the one who could get it scheduled on the floor and persuade the committee chairman to report it out. If the bill needed help in the House, Johnson was the one with a direct line to Speaker Sam Rayburn. And if the senator needed money for his next campaign (to ensure that he would remain a senator), Johnson was the one who could put in a good word with oilmen from his native Texas.

Johnson also put himself in a position to control committee assignments, which are the single biggest factor that shapes how a senator’s whole career plays out. For about a century, they had been handed out by seniority. Practically overnight, Johnson changed the system so that many seats were no longer being settled by seniority but rather negotiated by the party’s Steering committee, which Johnson controlled.  If you wanted a good seat, you had to do what Johnson wanted. In 1957, Estes Kefauver voted against Johnson on an important motion. That very same week, the highly coveted open seat on the Foreign Relations Committee, which Kefauver was expecting to get, was instead handed over to a far more junior senator named John F. Kennedy.

The real political genius of Lyndon Johnson was identifying and then gaining control over every possible source of leverage over his colleagues. Whatever a senator needed to survive, whether that was money, committee seats, or the passage of bills that matter to his home state, Johnson could give, and Johnson could withhold.

What the final bill that passes says depends on which one version actually comes to a vote, and with what final modifications. Whoever gets to set the agenda controls the outcome.  So you won’t  be surprised by who put himself in this position. Johnson’s main tool for setting the agenda was the unanimous consent agreement. By default, Senate debate is unlimited. A senator can talk about a bill for as long as he likes, and as he does so, he can also offer amendments that have nothing to do with that bill, each of which can stall the bill even further. A unanimous consent agreement sets those freedoms aside for a single bill: it fixes the allotted time for debate and constrains the opportunity to amend it. Earlier leaders rarely used such agreements, and even then, only after weeks of debate on a bill had already exhausted all the senators. Johnson made their use the norm in the Senate. He wouldn’t even allow a bill to reach the floor until such an agreement was in place.

Johnson wanted to control which bill reached the floor, and to keep the floor from changing anyone’s mind, because he wanted every vote settled in private beforehand, through the wheeling-and-dealing where his leverage worked best. The last thing he wanted was for a long, public debate on the merits of the bill to change a senator’s mind at the last minute, or for a surprise amendment to unravel a deal he had spent weeks painstakingly brokering. As Paul Douglas put it, under Johnson “all the action takes place offstage, before the play begins.”

Johnson made sure that as much of the Senate’s information as possible ran through him. He had every committee assign a staffer to tell him what was being drafted. His aides tracked what every senator was up to. And he spent his own days in the cloakroom and the hallways cajoling and listening to his colleagues. So he knew what each senator really wanted, what he would and wouldn’t give up to get it.

In any session, the Senate faces hundreds of possible bills and amendments. A senator’s vote on one bill can be traded for another senator’s vote on a different one, and any single bill can be amended a dozen ways to win someone over. So there’s an almost endless combination of possible deals to be made. Johnson made sure that he was the one instigating and brokering most of these deals. As a result, he could make sure that any deal left Johnson coming out ahead.

A good example here is how he got the Civil Rights Act of 1957 passed through the Senate. Johnson was desperate to make sure that a civil rights bill passed that year, even if it was weak. That’s because he wanted to be president, but no Southerner with his record of consistently voting against civil rights could hope to win the Democratic presidential nomination in 1960.

The problem was that there seemed to be no bill strong enough to win Northern liberals yet weak enough that the Southerners wouldn’t filibuster it. The sticking point was who would preside over the court cases where Southern electoral officials were accused of suppressing black voters. Southern Senators insisted on jury trials. But Northern Senators were livid - this would gut the whole bill. The entire point of the law was to combat the exclusion of black citizens from the voting rolls, but Southern states required jurors to be registered voters. An all-white Southern jury would never convict white registrars for turning away black voters.

Any version that one side could accept, the other would reject. A less creative legislator would have backed one side or fallen into the chasm between the two. But over the course of seven months, Johnson built a masterful deal that brought together wholly unrelated factions, and whose byproduct included the passage of this civil rights law. Western senators got a federal dam they had wanted for years between Idaho and Oregon. Midwestern Republicans, who had powerful railroad unions in their state, got the right to a jury trial extended to striking workers. And moderates got a clause guaranteeing that black citizens could serve on federal juries, so they could tell voters they had created a new civil right. Meanwhile the jury-trial guarantee for Southern registrars stayed in, which kept the bill weak enough that the Southerners agreed not to filibuster.

A dam in Idaho, protections for union workers, and federal jury rules had nothing to do with voting rights in the South. At least, not to anyone who lacked the shrewd inside understanding and political creativity of Lyndon Johnson.

Caro’s books are the best-written accounts of how political power actually works. But they are written so compellingly, with characters more vivid and stories more gripping than any novel, that it’s very easy to get so engrossed that you just keep turning the pages. And you never  step back to ask what lessons the stories teach about power.

I wanted to write this essay, both so that I could think through what those lessons actually are, and also so that you would have the context necessary to watch my interview with Caro and get as much out of it as I did when I spoke to him.
You’ll be able to watch the interview this Thursday. By the time you’re reading this, it might be already out. I hope you enjoy it!
